idiom_name: framework/target module with internal by default and public/open as the published surface
implementation_notes: In Swift the module is a first-class unit: everything in one target sees the default internal access level, public and open extend visibility to importers, and fileprivate and private narrow it inside the file. A domain module therefore becomes a target whose public API is the published surface while domain-internal types stay internal - nothing has to be annotated for the internals, only for what is published. When several related modules must share internals without exposing them to clients, the package access level (Swift 5.9, SE-0386) opens a declaration to the other modules of the same package, and package(set) narrows a setter further than its getter.
pitfalls: internal means the whole target - not a folder - so module-private is only as fine-grained as the targets you create.
A public type's members default to internal, so every published member must be marked public explicitly while an accidental public type exposes its whole surface by omission.

The compiler constrains access levels along signatures (a public function cannot use an internal type), so widening one declaration can force others to be widened - settle the published surface before writing framework code.
